h1: Beer with monsoon pakoras and bhajiyas on a rainy evening
title: Beer with Monsoon Pakoras and Bhajiyas | Craft Beer School
desc: Which beers suit monsoon pakoras: onion bhajiya, mirchi bhajji, batata vada, paneer and bread pakoras, plus how to serve beer on a rainy day.
teaser: It is raining, the kadhai is hot and the bhajiyas are coming. Here is the beer to have ready.
standfirst: Rain and fried snacks go together across India, usually with chai. Beer works just as well if you pick the right one. Here is our guide to pairing beer with monsoon pakoras.
sections: Why pakoras and beer get along

A pakora is a vegetable, paneer or bread dipped in a gram flour batter and fried in hot oil, around 170 to 180 °C. The batter puffs, browns and crisps. Inside, the filling steams. The result is fat, salt, a little spice and a lot of crunch.

Beer handles fried food better than almost any drink. Carbonation lifts oil off the tongue. Hop bitterness cuts through fat. Malt echoes the browned, toasty flavour of the batter. So the question is not whether beer works with pakoras. It is which beer works with which pakora.
Onion bhajiya and the classic pale lager

Kanda bhaji in Maharashtra, onion pakoda in the south, pyaz pakora in the north: the onion fritter is the monsoon classic. Thin onion slices, gram flour, green chilli, ajwain and coriander, fried into crisp, tangled clusters.

A crisp pale lager or a German Pilsner is the natural partner. A Pilsner at about 4.8% ABV with 25 to 40 IBU brings clean bitterness and a lightly floral hop that suits the ajwain. A Helles is softer if you want the sweetness of the onion to come through. Both should be cold: 4 to 6 °C.

Mirchi bhajji, large green chillies stuffed or slit and fried in batter, ranges from mild to fierce depending on the chilli. In Rajasthan the mirchi vada is stuffed with spiced potato.

Chilli heat and hop bitterness stack up, so skip the IPA. A hefeweizen, at 8 to 15 IBU with soft wheat and lots of carbonation, is the best friend of a hot mirchi bhajji. A witbier does a similar job with a citrus twist. If the chillies are mild, any pale lager will do.
Batata vada, paneer and bread pakoras

Batata vada, the spiced potato ball in gram flour batter, is the Mumbai monsoon snack. Bread pakora, paneer pakora and aloo pakora fill the same role across the north. These are heavier: more starch, more fat, more filling.

They can take a beer with more body. An amber lager or a Vienna lager brings toasty malt that matches the browned batter. A pale ale at 30 to 45 IBU, with citrus or floral hops, adds a fresh edge to a plate of bread pakoras with green chutney. Paneer pakora, mild and milky, is lovely with a Kölsch.

Then there is the oil itself. Pakoras fried in fresh oil taste clean and nutty. Oil that has been reused too many times smells stale and fishy. No beer can hide that. If a street stall's pakoras taste heavy and greasy, the problem is the kadhai, not your beer choice. At home, fry in small batches so the oil stays hot. Overcrowded oil drops in temperature, the batter soaks it up and the pakoras come out soggy.

Most pakoras arrive with green chutney (coriander, mint and green chilli), sweet tamarind chutney or tomato ketchup. These shift the balance. Tamarind adds sweetness and sourness, which makes a very bitter beer taste harsh. Green chutney adds herbal freshness, which suits hoppy beers well.

A simple rule: with sweet chutney, lean towards malty lagers and wheat beers. With green chutney, a Pilsner or pale ale shines. Our beer and food pairing basics explain why sweetness and bitterness interact this way.
Keeping beer cold on a humid evening

Monsoon evenings are often humid and warm, even when it is raining. A beer poured at 5 °C can be at 12 °C within twenty minutes in a thin glass on a balcony. Lagers lose their crispness as they warm, which matters with fried food.

Pour smaller amounts more often rather than one big glass. Keep bottles in the fridge or a bucket of ice and water, which chills faster than ice alone. Use a chilled glass but not a frozen one, because ice crystals make beer foam over and dull the flavour. Our guides to beer serving temperature and beer glassware go into more detail.
Set up a small pakora tasting

A rainy Sunday is a good excuse for a tasting at home. Fry three kinds of pakora: onion, mirchi and potato. Pour three beers: a Pilsner, a hefeweizen and an amber lager, in small glasses. Taste each pakora with each beer and note which you liked best. Offer masala chai to anyone who prefers it. Nobody drives after the tasting.

You will probably find the hefeweizen wins with the chilli, the Pilsner with the onion and the amber with the potato. If your results differ, that is interesting too. It means your palate weighs bitterness or sweetness differently, which is exactly what trained tasters learn to notice.

Your first step: next time it rains, fry a batch of onion bhajiyas and pour a cold Pilsner beside them. Then try the same bhajiya with a wheat beer.
faqs: What is the best beer with onion bhajiya?
A crisp Pilsner or pale lager served at 4 to 6 °C. Clean bitterness and carbonation cut the oil and suit the ajwain in the batter.
What beer goes with spicy mirchi bhajji?
A hefeweizen or witbier. They have low bitterness and high carbonation, so they calm chilli heat rather than adding to it.
How do I keep beer cold during the monsoon?
Chill bottles in a bucket of ice and water, pour small amounts at a time and use chilled but not frozen glasses.
